query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase compositionally complex high-entropy alloy, exposure to prolonged high service temperatures promotes localized grain-boundary segregation that triggers nucleation and growth of incoherent, brittle secondary phase precipitates at the grain boundaries, which in turn degrades toughness via intergranular fracture. This mechanism differs from conventional alloys where brittle behavior is predominantly driven by continuous grain-boundary films or coarse intermetallic precipitates.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, homogeneous high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi or similarly complex alloys) with coherent nanoscale precipitates and uniform grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging and/or prolonged high-temperature exposure to simulate service conditions.
generation.conditions: Aging at high but service-relevant temperatures (e.g., 700–900 °C) for extended durations under low strain-rate mechanical loading.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary segregation leading to the nucleation and growth of secondary phase precipitates with incoherent interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Thermal exposure induces local compositional fluctuations at the grain boundaries in high-entropy alloys. Unlike conventional alloys where brittle phases form as continuous films or coarse precipitates, in HEAs the complex matrix initially delays such effects. However, once a critical threshold of segregation is reached, even minute, incoherent precipitates can form at or near the grain boundaries, compromising intergranular cohesion and acting as crack initiation sites leading to brittle failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: After thermal aging, the HEA will exhibit a measurable reduction in fracture toughness (e.g., increased intergranular cracking and reduced crack propagation resistance) compared to the unaged baseline, and microstructural analysis will reveal localized, incoherent secondary phase particles at grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: The initial state with homogeneous microstructure showing high toughness and ductility, with uniformly distributed coherent nanoscale features.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold within service conditions characterized by high temperatures (700–900 °C) and low strain rates typical of prolonged operational environments; deviations might occur under rapid thermal cycling or very low service temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature/time threshold at which segregation becomes critical, as well as the interplay between the complex alloy composition and evolution of precipitate coherence, remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of initially single-phase HEA samples (using a method such as SLM or a processing route yielding homogeneous structures) and subject them to controlled thermal aging at 700–900 °C for varying durations. Include a control group maintained at room temperature. After aging, perform standardized fracture toughness tests (e.g., crack initiation and propagation tests) along with detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM, APT, and EBSD) focusing on grain-boundary chemistry and precipitate coherence.
measurements: Crack propagation rates under controlled loading
High-resolution TEM and APT measurements of grain-boundary composition and precipitate structure
Quantification of precipitate size, distribution, and interface coherence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal aging does not result in localized grain-boundary segregation and formation of incoherent, brittle secondary phase precipitates, or if no corresponding significant decrease in fracture toughness is observed compared to the unaged samples, then the hypothesis that such segregation drives brittleness in HEAs is falsified.

System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA).
